label: Rules governing nature need not be those of traditional mathematics
claim: Although theoretical science requires that the systems it studies follow definite rules, those rules need not be the equation-based rules of traditional mathematics; the more general rules embodied in simple computer programs are equally candidates for describing the natural world.
quote: the crucial realization that led me to develop the new kind of science in this book is that there is in fact no reason to think that systems like those we see in nature should follow only such traditional mathematical rules.
scope: rules underlying natural systems studied by the exact sciences
candidate_data: none known

label: Programs with very simple rules often behave in complex ways
claim: When simple computer programs are enumerated and run systematically, their behavior is often far from simple, and some of the very simplest programs produce behavior as complex as any known.
quote: despite the simplicity of their rules, the behavior of the programs was often far from simple. Indeed, even some of the very simplest programs that I looked at had behavior that was as complex as anything I had ever seen.
scope: simple programs such as elementary cellular automata, enumerated systematically
measurable_quantities: fraction of rules in an enumerated class whose evolution from simple initial conditions is non-repetitive and non-nested
compressibility or entropy of the generated patterns
candidate_data: Exhaustive simulation of elementary and other small-rule cellular automata with Mathematica, Python or Golly, plus published enumerations of elementary cellular automaton behavior.

label: Natural complexity arises because natural systems behave like typical programs
claim: The great complexity seen across physical, biological and other natural systems is explained by those systems operating like typical simple programs, which commonly produce complex behavior, rather than by any special or supernatural source of complexity.
quote: For all it takes is that systems in nature operate like typical programs and then it follows that their behavior will often be complex.
scope: complex-looking physical, biological and other natural systems
measurable_quantities: whether observed complex natural patterns can be reproduced by minimal-rule programs
statistical similarity between natural patterns and outputs of simple programs
candidate_data: Image and time-series collections of natural patterns (e.g. published shell-pattern image collections, snowflake image archives, turbulence data such as the Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database) compared against simple-program simulations.

label: Equation-based descriptions work for simple behavior but fail for complex behavior
claim: Describing behavior with mathematical equations succeeds for fairly simple behavior such as planetary motion but almost inevitably fails when behavior is more complex, and descriptions based on natural selection share this limitation; thinking in terms of programs allows meaningful statements about highly complex behavior.
quote: while their basic idea of describing behavior in terms of mathematical equations works well in cases like planetary motion where the behavior is fairly simple, it almost inevitably fails whenever the behavior is more complex.
scope: traditional mathematical and evolutionary explanations in the existing sciences
candidate_data: none known

label: The same basic forms of behavior recur in simple programs regardless of details
claim: Across the world of simple programs the same basic forms of behavior occur repeatedly almost independently of the underlying details of the rules, suggesting universal principles of overall behavior that should also apply to systems throughout nature.
quote: in the world of simple programs I have discovered that the same basic forms of behavior occur over and over again almost independent of underlying details.
scope: simple programs of many types (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, etc.) and, by extension, natural systems
measurable_quantities: distribution of behavior classes (uniform, repetitive, nested, random-looking, localized structures) across different program types
robustness of that distribution to changes in rule representation
candidate_data: Systematic enumeration of small cellular automata, Turing machines and other rule systems using public tools such as Mathematica or Python.

label: Simple programs yield a straightforward explanation of thermodynamic behavior
claim: The long-standing difficulty in understanding how thermodynamic behavior, including the Second Law of Thermodynamics, arises in physics can be resolved by a straightforward explanation drawn from the behavior of simple programs.
quote: For more than a century, for example, there has been confusion about how thermodynamic behavior arises in physics. Yet from my discoveries about simple programs I have developed a quite straightforward explanation.
scope: thermodynamics and statistical mechanics, specifically the basis of entropy increase
measurable_quantities: coarse-grained entropy over time in reversible simple-program models
agreement of such models with thermodynamic behavior of real gases
candidate_data: Simulations of reversible cellular automata and lattice-gas models with public tools, compared with standard thermodynamic property data such as the NIST Chemistry WebBook.

label: A single fundamental theory of physics may be built from simple programs
claim: Thinking in terms of simple programs should make it possible to construct a single, truly fundamental theory of physics from which space, time, quantum mechanics and all other known features of the universe emerge.
quote: thinking in terms of simple programs will make it possible to construct a single truly fundamental theory of physics, from which space, time, quantum mechanics and all the other known features of our universe will emerge.
scope: the fundamental structure of the universe
measurable_quantities: whether a candidate simple-program model reproduces observed particle spectra, spacetime dimensionality and gravitational behavior
candidate_data: Comparison of any specific candidate model against the PDG Review of Particle Physics and cosmological datasets such as the Planck Legacy Archive.

label: Universal computation is possible in systems with one-sentence rules
claim: Contrary to the assumption that computational universality requires elaborate systems like electronic computers, there exist systems whose rules can be stated in a single sentence that are nevertheless universal, able to perform any possible computation.
quote: there are systems whose rules are simple enough to describe in just one sentence that are nevertheless universal.
scope: simple rule systems such as elementary cellular automata and small Turing machines
measurable_quantities: existence of a proof of universality for a specified simple-rule system
size of the rule (number of states, colors, cases)
candidate_data: Published proofs and constructions in the computability literature, checkable by simulation with public tools.

label: Computational universality is far more common in abstract systems and nature
claim: Because universality can occur in systems with extremely simple rules, the phenomenon of universality is far more common and important, both among abstract systems and in nature, than previously supposed.
quote: this immediately suggests that the phenomenon of universality is vastly more common and important—in both abstract systems and nature—than has ever been imagined before.
scope: abstract rule systems and natural systems generally
measurable_quantities: fraction of simple rules in enumerated classes that can be proven or shown to be universal
candidate_data: Enumerations of small cellular automata and Turing machines combined with published universality results; no natural-system dataset known.

label: Principle of Computational Equivalence
claim: Whenever a system in essentially any domain shows behavior that is not obviously simple, that behavior can be regarded as a computation of equivalent sophistication to that of any other such system.
quote: whenever one sees behavior that is not obviously simple—in essentially any system—it can be thought of as corresponding to a computation of equivalent sophistication.
scope: essentially all systems, abstract and natural, whose behavior is not obviously simple
measurable_quantities: whether systems with non-simple behavior can be shown to be computationally universal
candidate_data: Published universality proofs for specific simple systems; no comprehensive dataset known.

label: Behavior looks complex because observers are computationally equivalent to it
claim: Simple programs appear complex to us because human perception and analysis are themselves computations that, by the Principle of Computational Equivalence, are no more sophisticated than those the programs perform.
quote: it is this equivalence between us as observers and the systems that we observe that makes the behavior of such systems seem to us complex.
scope: human perception and analysis of complex-looking systems
candidate_data: none known

label: Most systems with non-simple behavior are computationally irreducible
claim: Predicting a system's outcome by a mathematical shortcut is normally possible only for special systems with simple behavior; other systems are computationally irreducible, so their behavior can be found only by tracing each step with roughly as much computational effort as the system itself expends.
quote: such systems are computationally irreducible—so that in effect the only way to find their behavior is to trace each of their steps, spending about as much computational effort as the systems themselves.
scope: systems whose behavior is not obviously simple
measurable_quantities: existence or absence of predictive formulas or algorithms faster than direct simulation for specified systems
candidate_data: Computational experiments searching for shortcuts in specific cellular automata, plus computational complexity theory results; no general dataset known.

label: Computational irreducibility explains free will despite deterministic rules
claim: Computational irreducibility provides an explanation of how humans, even if they follow definite underlying rules, can meaningfully be said to have free will.
quote: it leads to an explanation of how we as humans—even though we may follow definite underlying rules—can still in a meaningful way show free will.
scope: human behavior and the philosophical question of free will
candidate_data: none known

label: Human intelligence is computationally no more sophisticated than simple programs
claim: In terms of computation or intelligence, humans are ultimately no more sophisticated than many simple programs and many systems in nature.
quote: when it comes to computation—or intelligence—we are in the end no more sophisticated than all sorts of simple programs, and all sorts of systems in nature.
scope: human cognition compared with simple programs and natural systems
candidate_data: none known

label: Complexity of simple abstract systems imposes fundamental limits on proof
claim: The complexity found in simple abstract systems leads to fundamental limitations on mathematical proof, of the kind hinted at by Gödel's Theorem, and these limitations are relevant well beyond the narrow scope of current mathematics.
quote: one of the consequences of this complexity is that it leads to fundamental limitations on the idea of proof that has been central to traditional mathematics.
scope: mathematical proof applied to abstract systems based on simple programs
measurable_quantities: existence of undecidable or unprovable statements about specific simple systems
candidate_data: Published undecidability results in logic and computability theory; no dataset known.

label: Simple programs capture how genetic programs generate biological forms
claim: Simple programs can reproduce many features of biological organisms and appear to capture essential mechanisms by which genetic programs generate observed biological forms, enabling new models and general abstract theories in biology.
quote: such programs can reproduce many features of biological organisms—and for example seem to capture some of the essential mechanisms through which genetic programs manage to generate the actual biological forms we see.
scope: biological morphogenesis and pigmentation patterns
measurable_quantities: fit between simple-program outputs and measured biological forms (shapes, pigment patterns, branching structures)
candidate_data: Published shell-pattern image collections, plant morphology datasets and developmental-biology imaging data compared with simulated outputs.

label: Sophisticated tasks need only extremely simple underlying rules
claim: Contrary to engineering experience, performing sophisticated tasks does not require correspondingly complicated basic rules; extremely simple underlying rules, potentially implementable directly at the atomic scale, are often sufficient.
quote: extremely simple underlying rules—that might for example potentially be implemented directly at the level of atoms—are often all that is needed.
scope: technology and engineered systems, including nanotechnology
measurable_quantities: minimal rule complexity sufficient for specified computational or physical tasks
feasibility of atomic-scale implementations
candidate_data: Results on minimal universal systems and molecular or DNA computing experiments in the published literature.

label: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions does not by itself produce complexity
claim: The sensitive dependence on initial conditions studied by chaos theory only makes complexity present in the initial conditions appear in large-scale behavior; it does not imply complex behavior when initial conditions are simple.
quote: all that it shows is that if there is complexity in the details of the initial conditions, then this complexity will eventually appear in the large-scale behavior of the system.
scope: chaotic dynamical systems
measurable_quantities: complexity of trajectories of chaotic maps started from simple (e.g. rational) initial conditions
candidate_data: Direct computation with standard chaotic maps such as the shift or logistic map using exact arithmetic in public tools.

label: Natural selection tends to oppose rather than generate complexity
claim: Darwinian natural selection does not clearly imply the generation of complexity and in many respects tends to oppose it; a different mechanism, the intrinsic complexity of simple programs, is responsible for most great complexity in biology.
quote: I will argue in this book that in many respects it tends to oppose complexity.
scope: biological evolution and the origin of biological complexity
measurable_quantities: change in pattern complexity under simulated selection on simple-program genomes
comparison of complexity in selected versus unselected traits
candidate_data: Artificial evolution simulations with public tools; comparative morphology data where available.

label: A rule-90-type cellular automaton produces a nested self-similar pattern
claim: A one-dimensional cellular automaton in which each cell becomes black when exactly one of its two neighbors was black (rule 90), started from a single black cell, produces an intricate but regular nested pattern made of triangular pieces that are smaller copies of the whole.
quote: it actually consists of many nested triangular pieces that all have exactly the same form.
scope: elementary cellular automaton rule 90 from a single black cell
measurable_quantities: self-similarity of the pattern
fractal dimension of the pattern
candidate_data: Direct simulation of elementary cellular automata with public tools.

label: Rule 30 from a single black cell produces an irregular, complex pattern
claim: The elementary cellular automaton rule 30, started from a single black cell, produces a highly irregular and complex pattern with almost no overall regularity, rather than a uniform, repetitive or nested one.
quote: Rather than getting a simple regular pattern as we might expect, the cellular automaton instead produces a pattern that seems extremely irregular and complex.
scope: elementary cellular automaton rule 30 from a single black cell
measurable_quantities: compressibility of the pattern
presence or absence of periodicity or nesting
candidate_data: Direct simulation of rule 30 with public tools such as Mathematica, Python or Golly.

label: Simple rules with simple initial conditions can yield highly complex behavior
claim: As a general phenomenon, a system with simple underlying rules started from simple initial conditions can nevertheless show highly complex behavior.
quote: even though the underlying rules for a system are simple, and even though the system is started from simple initial conditions, the behavior that the system shows can nevertheless be highly complex.
scope: simple programs and other systems with simple rules and simple initial conditions
measurable_quantities: complexity measures of output as a function of rule and initial-condition size
candidate_data: Systematic simulation of enumerated simple programs with public tools.

label: Complexity from simple rules accounts for most complexity in nature
claim: The generation of complex behavior from simple rules and simple initial conditions is ultimately responsible for most of the complexity seen in nature.
quote: I will argue that it is this basic phenomenon that is ultimately responsible for most of the complexity that we see in nature.
scope: complex phenomena throughout the natural world
measurable_quantities: proportion of well-studied complex natural phenomena successfully modeled by simple deterministic rules versus random inputs or complex mechanisms
candidate_data: none known

label: Rule 30's center column shows no deviation from randomness over a million steps
claim: The sequence of cell colors directly below the initial black cell in rule 30 does not repeat in its first million steps, and statistical tests show no meaningful deviation from perfect randomness.
quote: in the first million steps in this sequence, for example, it never repeats, and indeed none of the tests I have ever done on it show any meaningful deviation at all from perfect randomness.
scope: center column of elementary cellular automaton rule 30 from a single black cell
measurable_quantities: period of the center-column sequence
results of standard randomness test batteries
frequency of black versus white cells
candidate_data: Direct computation of the rule 30 center column (also listed in OEIS) tested with the NIST SP 800-22 statistical test suite or TestU01.

label: Some cellular automata make even average properties hard to predict
claim: Some simple cellular automata, such as rule 110, are more complex than random-looking ones like rule 30: they mix regular regions with interacting localized structures, so that even average properties of their behavior become very difficult to predict.
quote: there are cellular automata whose behavior is in effect still more complex—and in which even such averages become very difficult to predict.
scope: elementary cellular automata with localized structures, especially rule 110
measurable_quantities: density of black cells over time
number and types of localized structures
variance of averages across runs
candidate_data: Direct simulation of rule 110 with public tools.

label: Rule 110's fate can be determined only by running it
claim: Whether the localized structures in rule 110 eventually annihilate into a regular pattern or proliferate into randomness apparently cannot be determined in advance; the only reliable method is to run the cellular automaton for as many steps as needed.
quote: The only sure way to answer these questions, it seems, is just to run the cellular automaton for as many steps as are needed
scope: elementary cellular automaton rule 110 and similar systems
measurable_quantities: existence of any predictive shortcut for rule 110 evolution faster than direct simulation
candidate_data: Direct simulation of rule 110 and computational-complexity results on cellular automaton prediction.

label: Rule 110 from one black cell becomes periodic with period 240 after about 2780 steps
claim: Rule 110 started from a single black cell resolves after about 2780 steps: one localized structure survives and interacts with periodic stripes from the left to give behavior that repeats every 240 steps.
quote: the outcome is finally clear after about 2780 steps: one structure survives, and that structure interacts with the periodic stripes coming from the left to produce behavior that repeats every 240 steps.
scope: elementary cellular automaton rule 110 from a single black cell
measurable_quantities: step at which the right-hand region becomes periodic
period of the eventual behavior
candidate_data: Direct simulation of rule 110 with public tools.

label: Identical cell rules yield diverse behaviors through different configurations
claim: Even though every cell of a cellular automaton follows the same rule, different configurations of cell colors can collectively produce many different kinds of behavior, such as regular backgrounds and distinct localized structures.
quote: even though individual cells follow the same rule, different configurations of cells with different sequences of colors can together produce all sorts of different kinds of behavior.
scope: cellular automata, exemplified by rule 110
measurable_quantities: catalog of distinct localized structures and background patterns produced by one rule
candidate_data: Direct simulation of rule 110 and published catalogs of its localized structures.

label: Intuition that complex results need complex plans comes from engineering
claim: The intuition that complex objects require complex construction plans fails because it derives from engineering, where designers restrict themselves to systems whose behavior they can understand and predict, a constraint nature does not share.
quote: Yet to do this reliably, we have to restrict ourselves to systems whose behavior we can readily understand and predict—for unless we can foresee how a system will behave, we cannot be sure that the system will do what we want.
scope: human intuition about complexity and the practice of engineering
candidate_data: none known

label: Systems with simple rules and complex behavior are very common in nature
claim: Because nature is not constrained to predictable designs, systems whose simple rules produce complex behavior, like rule 30 and rule 110, are very common in nature.
quote: one of the important conclusions of this book is that such systems are actually very common in nature.
scope: natural systems generally
measurable_quantities: frequency with which complex natural phenomena are well modeled by simple-rule systems
candidate_data: none known

label: Complex cellular-automaton-like patterns are absent from historical ornament
claim: Historical ornamental art contains many repetitive patterns and some nested ones, but the more complicated patterns produced by simple cellular automata such as rule 30 never appear to have been used.
quote: Repetitive patterns are common and some nested patterns are seen, but the more complicated kinds of patterns discussed in this chapter do not ever appear to have been used.
scope: historical ornamental art across cultures
measurable_quantities: occurrence of non-repetitive, non-nested rule-based patterns in catalogued historical ornament
candidate_data: Museum collection databases with ornament images (e.g. the Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access collection) and published pattern catalogs.

label: Computers enable discoveries beyond working out mathematical equations
claim: Computers are not limited to computing the consequences of mathematical equations; directly studying the behavior of even the simplest computer programs yields fundamental scientific discoveries.
quote: computers are not just limited to working out consequences of mathematical equations. And indeed, what we have seen in this chapter is that there are fundamental discoveries that can be made if one just studies directly the behavior of even some of the very simplest computer programs.
scope: the role of computers in basic science
candidate_data: none known

label: Unknown phenomena are found only by systematic, preconception-free experiments
claim: Phenomena not already known to exist can be found only by very systematic and general experiments whose results are examined with as few preconceptions as possible.
quote: the only way to find phenomena that one does not already know exist is to do very systematic and general experiments, and then to look at the results with as few preconceptions as possible.
scope: scientific methodology, especially computer experiments
candidate_data: none known

label: Lack of adequate computers delayed discovery of complexity from simple rules
claim: A main reason that complexity from simple programs was not discovered before the 1980s is that computer technology powerful enough for the required large-scale exploratory experiments did not yet exist, together with a lack of intuition drawn from practical computing.
quote: one of the main reasons that the discoveries I describe in this chapter were not made before the 1980s is just that computer technology did not yet exist powerful enough to do the kinds of exploratory experiments that were needed.
scope: history of science and computing
candidate_data: none known

label: It is usually very hard to foresee what even a simple program will do
claim: Practical computing shows that it is usually very difficult to foresee the behavior of even a simple program, which is why software bugs are so common; the simple structure of cellular automaton rules likewise does not make their behavior easy to predict.
quote: from experience in practical computing one knows that it is usually very difficult to foresee what even a simple program will do.
scope: simple programs, including software and cellular automata
measurable_quantities: success rate of predicting program outputs without execution
bug rates relative to program size
candidate_data: Public software defect datasets (e.g. Defects4J) and program-comprehension studies in the software engineering literature.

label: Primes follow simple generating rules yet are distributed seemingly randomly
claim: The prime numbers, though generated by simple rules, have a distribution that seems in many respects random, an early instance of complexity from simple rules that mathematics largely neglected in favor of proving regularities.
quote: The rules for generating primes are simple, yet their distribution seems in many respects random.
scope: distribution of prime numbers
measurable_quantities: statistics of prime gaps
deviations of prime counts from smooth approximations
candidate_data: Prime tables and prime-gap sequences in the OEIS and public prime databases, analyzed with standard number-theory software.

label: The digits of pi appear random despite simple rules for computing them
claim: The digit sequence of pi, produced by simple computational rules, appears quite random, illustrating that simple rules can produce complex results.
quote: By the 1700s more than a hundred digits of π had been computed, and they appeared quite random.
scope: decimal digit sequence of pi
measurable_quantities: digit frequencies
results of randomness tests on digit blocks
candidate_data: Published trillion-digit computations of pi and the OEIS digit sequence, tested with standard randomness test suites.

label: Complexity from simple programs was never discovered before despite many hints
claim: Although there were many hints over several centuries, including primes, digits of pi, iterated maps and the Game of Life, the basic phenomenon of simple programs producing complex behavior was never identified before Wolfram's work.
quote: despite many hints over the course of several centuries, the basic phenomenon that I have described in this chapter was never discovered before.
scope: history of science and mathematics
candidate_data: none known
